chapter: Struttin' Time, chronology and Chicago singers
title: Harold Browning, and getting the Chicago Defender in Europe
summary: Browning, her friend, was the Defender's London correspondent; she wrote for it and collected copies at American Express in Paris; she names Defender and New York Age figures.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Browning was the singer. He's a good friend of mine. And when I go to California, I always stop with Mr. and Mrs. Browning.
And he was in England too.
Oh, yes. Well, you see, that was Browning and Starr, Henry Starr.
And he also worked as a sort of a London correspondent for the Chicago Defender.
Chicago Defender, yes. Well, at that time I used to give -- I used to write a lot of stuff into the Chicago Defender about what was going on.
Did you get the Chicago Defender in England?

Always -- I got it everyplace. You had to go down -- you had to go down to the American Express on Rue Scribe to get it, and I used to go down there all the time. Everybody did. We -- of course, if you didn't get there early, you couldn't get it, because the white people bought it up.

White people bought up the Tattler and the -- all the papers, the colored papers, and I tell you, you know, Mr. Abbott, Robert Abbott was the owner of Chicago Defender, and he -- well, he was a nice man, and he always saw that everything was up to the minute in the paper, you
know? And he had some wonderful writers -- critics and all, you know, they were wonderful, wonderful people.

There was Frank Young. He was there -- and Phil Jones -- Chicago Defender -- Al Munro. They were with the Chicago Defender. And then now in New Y ork there was a New York Age. Fred Moore had the New York Age. Amsterdam was Sadie Warren. She had the Amsterdam, and her daughter Odessa had the big millinery store, had the big hat shop in --
